intro: A research ship off Louisiana lowers an oxygen probe and finds bottom water where nothing can breathe. A spectrophotometer in Antarctica shows a protective layer of ozone thinning by a third each spring. An observatory on a Hawaiian volcano records the carbon dioxide in the air climbing, year after year, in a sawtooth line. None of these were expected. Each was a measurement someone took carefully and then had to explain, and each traced back, through a chain of cause and effect, to ordinary human activity: growing corn, keeping food cold, driving to work.

Environmental science is the study of those chains. It borrows from ecology, chemistry, geology, physics and economics to ask how energy and matter move through Earth's systems, what happens when people change the flows, and what can be done about it. It is a science of stocks and flows, feedback loops and tipping points, of soil that takes centuries to build and aquifers that take decades to drain. It is also a science that ends in decisions: laws, treaties, budgets and the design of the places people live.

By the end of this unit you should be able to trace a nitrogen atom from an Illinois cornfield to the Gulf of Mexico, explain why a chlorine atom in the stratosphere matters to your skin, read the evidence for a warming climate and say what is certain and what is not, and compare the tools a society can use to fix an environmental problem. You will also be able to say, with evidence, why some of those problems have been solved and others have not.
bigQuestion: How do we discover that human activity is changing Earth's systems, and how do we decide what to do about it?

timeline.t: John Tyndall measures which gases absorb heat radiation and finds water vapor and carbon dioxide do
Svante Arrhenius calculates that doubling carbon dioxide would warm the planet by several degrees
Fritz Haber synthesizes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen, the basis of synthetic fertilizer
After Dust Bowl storms darken the sky, Congress creates the Soil Conservation Service
Charles David Keeling begins precise carbon dioxide measurements at Mauna Loa, Hawaii
Congress passes the Clean Air Act and the Environmental Protection Agency is created
The Clean Water Act requires permits for any pipe discharging pollution into U.S. waters
Molina and Rowland warn that CFCs will destroy stratospheric ozone
British scientists report the Antarctic ozone hole; yearly mapping of the Gulf dead zone begins
Nations sign the Montreal Protocol to phase out ozone-destroying chemicals
Federal and state agencies set a goal to shrink the Gulf hypoxic zone to about 1,900 square miles
Illinois adopts its Nutrient Loss Reduction Strategy; nations sign the Paris climate agreement

words.d: the amount stored in a system and the rates at which it enters or leaves; the basic tools of systems thinking
a loop that pushes back against change and keeps a system steady
a loop in which a change causes more of the same change, so the system runs away
a feeding level in an ecosystem; only about a tenth of the energy passes from one level to the next
nutrient overload in water that causes algae blooms, decay and loss of dissolved oxygen
an underground layer of rock or sediment that stores water and can supply wells
a resource such as a mineral or fossil fuel that nature does not replace on a human time scale
pollution from a single identifiable place such as a pipe, as opposed to diffuse runoff
warming caused by gases that absorb infrared heat from Earth's surface and send part of it back down
reducing the causes of climate change, mainly by cutting greenhouse gas emissions
adjusting buildings, farms and cities to cope with climate changes that cannot be prevented
a cost of an activity that falls on people who were not part of the deal, such as pollution downwind

test.q: A city's reservoir has held steady for decades. Pumping rises 10 percent while inflow stays the same. What should you expect?
choices: The reservoir level drops immediately to zero
The level falls gradually over years, because a stock responds slowly to a change in flow
Nothing changes, because the reservoir is a closed system
Inflow rises to match the new pumping
test.why: Output now exceeds input, so the stock declines, but slowly, which is why such problems build unnoticed.

test.q: Which situation shows a tipping point?
choices: A thermostat keeping a room at 20 degrees
A pond that turns cloudy with algae and stays cloudy even after fertilizer runoff returns to normal
A prairie regrowing after rain returns
A lake at dynamic equilibrium
test.why: Past a threshold, positive feedback holds the pond in its new state even when the original push is removed.

test.q: Why can a prairie support far more grasshoppers than hawks?
choices: Hawks eat plants
Grasshoppers live longer
Roughly 90 percent of the energy is lost as heat at each trophic level
Hawks are larger and need less food
test.why: Energy passes up the food chain at only about ten percent efficiency, so top predators are necessarily few.

test.q: The Haber-Bosch process is linked to the Gulf of Mexico dead zone because it
choices: produces the phosphorus in detergents
warms the Gulf water
made mass production of nitrogen fertilizer possible, much of which runs off fields into rivers
removes oxygen from the Mississippi
test.why: Industrial nitrogen fixation supplies the fertilizer whose runoff feeds algae blooms that deplete Gulf oxygen.

test.q: What sequence creates the hypoxic zone each summer?
choices: Nutrients from the river feed algae; algae die and sink; bacteria decomposing them use up oxygen; stratified water blocks resupply
Oil spills poison the water; fish die; bacteria multiply
Warm water holds no oxygen; fish leave; algae grow
Salt water sinks; fresh water floats; fish suffocate in the fresh layer
test.why: Eutrophication plus summer stratification removes oxygen from the bottom layer of the Gulf near the river mouth.

test.q: The Ogallala Aquifer is being drawn down because
choices: climate change stopped rainfall on the Plains
the water flows away into the Mississippi
irrigation pumping far exceeds the aquifer's slow natural recharge
farmers abandoned the region
test.why: With little rain reaching the ancient groundwater, heavy pumping since the 1950s has lowered the water table by over 100 feet in places.

test.q: Which best describes a trade-off of wind and solar power compared with natural gas?
choices: They emit more carbon dioxide
They require radioactive waste storage
They depend on fossil fuel mining
Their output is intermittent, so a grid needs storage, backup or long transmission lines
test.why: Wind and sun are not available on demand; gas is, but it emits carbon dioxide and other pollutants.

test.q: Why has U.S. air grown much cleaner since 1970 while the economy grew?
choices: Factories moved to other states
The Clean Air Act set enforceable health-based limits and required cleaner cars and fuels
People stopped driving
Weather patterns changed
test.why: EPA data show large declines in regulated pollutants and in children's blood lead after standards and technology requirements took effect.

test.q: Which pollution source is hardest for the Clean Water Act's permit system to control?
choices: Fertilizer runoff from thousands of farm fields
A sewage treatment plant's outfall
A factory discharge pipe
A single leaking storage tank
test.why: Permits work on identifiable point sources; nonpoint runoff from a wide area has no pipe to regulate.

test.q: Why was the ozone problem easier to solve than climate change?
choices: Ozone loss was not really harmful
It involved a few chemicals with available substitutes rather than the fuels that power everything
Only one country produced CFCs
The ozone hole closed on its own
test.why: The Montreal Protocol succeeded because replacements existed and the change was manageable; carbon dioxide comes from the core of the energy system.

choices: nitrogen and oxygen trap most of Earth's heat
water vapor and carbon dioxide absorb heat radiation while nitrogen and oxygen let it pass
carbon dioxide reflects sunlight back to space
ozone warms the surface
test.why: His measurements identified the gases responsible for the greenhouse effect over 160 years ago.

test.q: How do scientists know the extra carbon dioxide in the air comes from fossil fuels?
choices: Because volcanoes have gone quiet
Because the ocean is releasing carbon dioxide
Because fossil carbon has a distinct isotope signature that the atmosphere has shifted toward, and the ocean is absorbing carbon, not releasing it
Because carbon dioxide levels were higher in 1800
test.why: The lack of carbon-14 and low carbon-13 in fossil carbon show up in the air exactly as expected, and the ocean is a sink.

test.q: Which statement about climate uncertainty is accurate?
choices: Whether Earth has warmed is still an open question
The cause of warming is unknown
Models cannot reproduce past temperatures
Warming and its human cause are well established, while the pace of ice loss and regional rainfall changes carry real uncertainty
test.why: Good science separates settled findings from areas of active research and states the range for each.

test.q: Planting street trees in a neighborhood that suffered most in the 1995 Chicago heat wave is an example of
choices: mitigation
cap and trade
carbon accounting
adaptation, and also environmental justice
test.why: Trees reduce heat exposure for a community that bore a disproportionate burden; they adjust to warming rather than reduce emissions.

test.q: A state wants to cut sulfur dioxide by a fixed total at the lowest cost. Which tool guarantees the total and lets cheap cuts happen first?
choices: Cap and trade
A uniform rule for every plant
A subsidy for coal
Voluntary pledges
test.why: The cap fixes the total; trading lets plants with low costs do the cutting, as the 1990 acid rain program showed.

write.prompt: Take a position: should Illinois require, rather than encourage, farm practices that reduce nitrogen loss to rivers? Write a claim, support it with at least three pieces of evidence from this unit, and explain the reasoning that connects them.
tips: State your claim in one clear sentence, including whether rules, payments or a market would work best.
Use evidence such as the dead zone's size, the sources of nitrogen, what cover crops and wetlands do, and how the Clean Air Act or Montreal Protocol succeeded.
Explain the reasoning with stock-and-flow logic: which flow changes, and why the Gulf would respond slowly.
Address the other side: costs to farmers, the limits of nonpoint regulation, and who should pay.
Be honest about uncertainty: how much loss each practice prevents varies with weather and management.
